summary: Monogamous marriage did not arise from romantic ideals, but as an economic system created so men could guarantee legitimate heirs to inherit their private wealth.
context: Engels analyzes the economic origins of patriarchal marriage. When individual men accumulated wealth (livestock, land, slaves), they demanded guaranteed paternity so their accumulated private property could pass directly to their biological offspring.

It was the first form of the family to be based, not on natural, but on
economic cond
summary: Monogamy was the first family structure driven primarily by property rights and economic inheritance rather than mutual affection or communal clan ties.
context: In early communal societies, resources and child-rearing were shared by the entire clan. Monogamous domestic units developed only after private property disrupted collective living.

summary: The subjugation of women in patriarchal marriage was the earliest form of class oppression in human history, establishing the template for all subsequent economic exploitation.
context: Engels directly links gender oppression to class oppression. In early human history, women held respected positions in communal clans. The rise of private property restricted women to domestic isolation, transforming wives into dependent housekeepers.

summary: Historically, strict marital fidelity was enforced upon women to safeguard property inheritance, while male infidelity was socially tolerated or institutionally accommodated.
context: Engels highlights the structural double standard of traditional monogamous marriage systems, where women were legally bound to domestic chastity while men had legal or social access to concubinage and prostitution.
